items.title: Section: The Exception Applied to Killing — Better That I Go to Hell Than He

items.zh: 謂如菩薩見劫盜賊，為貪財故，欲殺多生，或復欲害大德聲聞、獨覺、菩薩，或復欲造多無間業。見是事已，發心思惟：我若斷彼惡眾生命，墮那落迦，如其不斷，無間業成，當受大苦；我寧殺彼墮那落迦，終不令其受無間苦。如是菩薩意樂思惟，於彼眾生或以善心、或無記心，知此事已，為當來故深生慚愧，以憐愍心而斷彼命。由是因緣，於菩薩戒無所違犯，生多功德。
items.en: Suppose a bodhisattva sees a bandit who, driven by greed for wealth, intends to kill many beings, or intends to harm an accomplished śrāvaka, solitary realiser, or bodhisattva, or intends to commit one of the deeds that ripen into the uninterrupted hell. Seeing this, the bodhisattva reflects: "If I take this evil being's life, I myself will fall into hell. But if I do not, his uninterrupted-hell-ripening deed will be completed, and he will suffer greatly for it. I would rather kill him and fall into hell myself than let him suffer the uninterrupted torment." Reflecting with this resolve, and knowing the matter clearly through a wholesome or karmically neutral mind, the bodhisattva — feeling deep and genuine shame at what is to come, and moved purely by compassion — takes that being's life. Through this very cause, the bodhisattva incurs no violation of the bodhisattva precepts, and instead generates substantial merit.

items.title: Section: Deposing a Tyrannical Ruler or Minister

items.zh: 又如菩薩，見有增上增上宰官，上品暴惡，於諸有情無有慈愍，專行逼惱。菩薩見已，起憐愍心，發生利益安樂意樂，隨力所能，若廢、若黜增上等位。由是因緣，於菩薩戒無所違犯，生多功德。
items.en: Suppose further that a bodhisattva sees a supremely powerful king or a supremely powerful minister acting with extreme, top-grade cruelty, utterly without compassion for any being, devoted entirely to oppressing and tormenting others. Seeing this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion, generates the resolve to bring benefit and ease, and, to whatever extent their own strength and ability permit, has that ruler or minister deposed or removed from their position of power. Through this very cause, the bodhisattva incurs no violation of the bodhisattva precepts, and instead generates substantial merit.

items.title: Section: Forcibly Reclaiming What Belongs to the Three Jewels

items.zh: 又如菩薩，見劫盜賊奪他財物，若僧伽物、窣堵波物，取多物已執為己有，縱情受用。菩薩見已，起憐愍心，於彼有情發生利益安樂意樂，隨力所能，逼而奪取，勿令受用如是財故，當受長夜無義無利。由此因緣，所奪財寶，若僧伽物，還復僧伽；窣堵波物，還窣堵波；若有情物，還復有情。又見眾主、或園林主，取僧伽物、窣堵波物，言是己有，縱情受用。菩薩見已，思擇彼惡，起憐愍心，勿令因此邪受用業，當受長夜無義無利，隨力所能廢其所主。菩薩如是雖不與取，而無違犯，生多功德。
items.en: Suppose further that a bodhisattva sees a bandit seize another's property — property belonging to the monastic community, or to a stupa — and, having taken a great deal of it, treats it as personal possession, consuming it freely. Seeing this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion, generates the resolve to bring that being benefit and ease, and, to whatever extent their strength permits, forcibly takes it back... Through this cause, the reclaimed wealth is returned precisely to its owner: if it belonged to the community, it is returned to the community; if to a stupa, to the stupa; if to a being, to that being. ...Suppose too the bodhisattva sees a community steward or a groundskeeper of monastic property take goods belonging to the community or a stupa, declare them personal possessions, and consume them freely. Seeing this, the bodhisattva weighs the wrongness of the act, gives rise to a heart of compassion, and — so that this wrongful consuming will not bring the steward long, meaningless suffering — to whatever extent their strength permits, removes that person from their position of trust. Though the bodhisattva has in this way taken what was not given, there is no violation, and substantial merit is generated.

items.title: Section: An Exception for Lay Bodhisattvas Only — Sexual Misconduct

items.zh: 又如菩薩處在居家，見有母邑現無繫屬，習婬欲法，繼心菩薩求非梵行。菩薩見已，作意思惟：勿令心恚，多生非福，若隨其欲，便得自在，方便安處令種善根，亦當令其捨不善業。住慈愍心，行非梵行。雖習如是穢染之法，而無所犯，多生功德。出家菩薩，為護聲聞聖所教誡，令不壞滅，一切不應行非梵行。
items.en: Suppose further that a bodhisattva living at home sees a woman presently belonging to no one else, given over to habitual sensual craving, who becomes infatuated with the bodhisattva and seeks intimacy. Seeing this, the bodhisattva reflects: "If I do not do as she wishes, resentment will arise in her heart and much that is unwholesome will follow; if I comply with her wish, she will find ease, and I can skilfully settle her in a way that plants wholesome roots, and eventually lead her to abandon the unwholesome altogether." Abiding in a heart of compassion, the bodhisattva engages in the act. Though this involves what is ordinarily an impure and defiling deed, there is no violation, and substantial merit is generated. ... An ordained bodhisattva, however, in order to protect the śrāvaka precepts' own sacred instruction from being undermined, must never engage in such conduct under any circumstance whatsoever.

items.zh: 又如菩薩為多有情解脫命難、囹圄縛難、刖手足難、劓鼻刵耳剜眼等難，雖諸菩薩為自命難，亦不正知說於妄語，然為救脫彼有情故，知而思擇，故說妄語。以要言之，菩薩唯觀有情義利，非無義利，自無染心，唯為饒益諸有情故，覆想正知而說異語。說是語時，於菩薩戒無所違犯，生多功德。
items.en: Suppose further that a bodhisattva, in order to free many beings from mortal danger, imprisonment, or the danger of having their hands and feet cut off, their nose or ears sliced off, or their eyes gouged out, will — though such a bodhisattva would never knowingly speak falsely even to save their own life — for the sake of rescuing those beings, knowingly and deliberately choose to speak falsely. In short, a bodhisattva considers only what genuinely benefits beings, never what lacks benefit, and, the mind itself entirely free of any self-interested motive, purely to bring beings benefit, deliberately sets aside their own true perception and knowingly speaks words other than the truth. In speaking such words, the bodhisattva incurs no violation of the bodhisattva precepts, and instead generates substantial merit.

items.title: Section: Divisive Speech to Break a Harmful Friendship, and Harsh Speech to Correct Open Wrongdoing

items.zh: 又如菩薩，見諸有情為惡朋友之所攝受，親愛不捨。菩薩見已，起憐愍心，發生利益安樂意樂，隨能隨力說離間語，令離惡友，捨相親愛，勿令有情由近惡友，當受長夜無義無利。菩薩如是以饒益心說離間語，乖離他愛，無所違犯，生多功德。又如菩薩，見諸有情為行越路，非理而行，出麁惡語，猛利訶擯，方便令其出不善處安立善處。菩薩如是以饒益心，於諸有情出麁惡語，無所違犯，生多功德。
items.en: Suppose further that a bodhisattva sees beings taken in by a harmful friend, bound to that friend by affection they will not let go. Seeing this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion, generates the resolve to bring benefit and ease, and, to whatever extent their ability allows, speaks words designed to divide the two, freeing the being from the harmful friend and severing the mutual attachment... Speaking such divisive words with a heart of genuine benefit in this way, and thereby severing another's affection, the bodhisattva incurs no violation, and substantial merit is generated. Suppose further that a bodhisattva sees beings acting outside the bounds of proper conduct, behaving unreasonably, and addresses them with harsh, forceful reproach, skilfully drawing them out of an unwholesome place and settling them in a wholesome one. Speaking such harsh words to beings with a heart of genuine benefit in this way, the bodhisattva incurs no violation, and substantial merit is generated.

items.title: Section: Idle Talk as Skilful Rapport — The Eighth Exception Closes the Set

items.zh: 又如菩薩，見諸有情信樂倡伎、吟詠、歌諷，或有信樂王、賊、飲食、婬蕩街衢無義之論，菩薩於中皆悉善巧，於彼有情起憐愍心，發生利益安樂意樂，現前為作綺語相應種種倡伎、吟詠、歌諷、王、賊、飲食、婬衢等論，令彼有情歡喜引攝、自在隨屬，方便獎導出不善處安立善處。菩薩如是現行綺語，無所違犯，生多功德。
items.en: Suppose further that a bodhisattva sees beings who delight in performance, song, and verse, or who delight in talk of rulers, of bandits, of food and drink, of romance, or the meaningless chatter of the street corner. Genuinely skilled in all of it, the bodhisattva, moved by compassion for these beings and the resolve to bring them benefit and ease, engages right there in exactly this kind of idle talk — performance, song, verse, talk of rulers, bandits, food, and romance — so that these beings, delighted, are drawn in and freely attach themselves to the bodhisattva, who then skilfully guides and leads them out of an unwholesome way of living and into a wholesome one. Engaging in idle talk in this way, the bodhisattva incurs no violation, and substantial merit is generated.

blocks.text: The treatise gives concrete examples of the "skilful exception". They are among the most debated passages in Buddhist ethics, and should be read with care. Every case has the same structure: a grave harm to others is imminent; the bodhisattva acts from compassion, with a wholesome mind, accepting the karmic cost for themselves.

A bodhisattva sees "a bandit who, for wealth, intends to kill many beings", or to harm noble ones, or to commit a deed that leads to the worst hell. "If I kill him, I will fall into hell. But if I do not, he will suffer far worse. I would rather kill him and fall into hell myself." "With deep shame at what is to come, moved purely by compassion", the bodhisattva acts. Note the motive: compassion for the bandit himself, as well as for his victims. The treatise says the bodhisattva knows the situation "through a wholesome or neutral mind"; Master Cháng Bǎi: knowing through absorption is wholesome, through supernormal power neutral. Either way, it is real knowledge, not suspicion.
"A king or minister of extreme cruelty, without compassion for any being": the bodhisattva may remove them from power.

A bandit who has seized the community's or a stupa's property: the bodhisattva takes it back and returns it "to the community, to the stupa, or to its owners". Venerable Miào Jìng: today, the abbot would call a board meeting.

A lay bodhisattva and an unattached woman who is infatuated: to prevent her resentment and lead her towards the good, the bodhisattva may comply. "An ordained bodhisattva, to protect the śrāvaka teaching, must never do so."

subs.head: Lying, dividing, harsh and idle speech

blocks.text: To save beings from death, prison, or mutilation, a bodhisattva may lie. To free someone from a harmful friend, divisive speech. To correct open wrongdoing, harsh words. To draw in those who love songs and gossip, idle talk, "and then lead them into the Dharma".

These passages do not loosen ethics; they deepen them. The bodhisattva breaks the letter of a precept only to keep its purpose (protecting beings) and accepts the consequences. The commentators restrict it to the highly advanced; for everyone else, the precepts stand.

quiz.q: Seeing a bandit about to kill many and commit deeds leading to the uninterrupted hell, how does the bodhisattva reflect?
options: better that I kill him and fall into hell than let him suffer the uninterrupted hell
quiz.why: "I would rather kill him and fall into hell than let him suffer in the uninterrupted hell." With compassion the bodhisattva takes the life, incurring no violation and much merit. Master Cháng Bǎi: the bodhisattva is like a good physician, killing with a mind to benefit.

quiz.q: The bodhisattva takes the life "with a wholesome mind or a neutral mind." How do the lectures distinguish them?
options: knowing others' minds arising from absorption is wholesome; what arises from supernormal transformation is neutral
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: mind-reading arising from absorption is a wholesome mind; what arises from supernormal transformation is a neutral mind. Venerable Miào Jìng: concentration is wholesome; when supernormal power issues forth, it is called neutral.

quiz.q: Having forcibly reclaimed what a bandit seized, what does the bodhisattva do with it?
options: return community property to the community, stupa property to the stupa, beings' property to the beings
quiz.why: "If it is property of the community, it goes back to the community; if of a stupa, to the stupa; if of beings, back to them." Master Cháng Bǎi's example: many monastics fail to arrange their estates, and after death their lay relatives take ownership.

quiz.q: "A head of the community or a keeper of the grounds who claims community or stupa property as their own." How do the two lectures explain "zhòng zhǔ"?
options: Miào Jìng: the abbot of a temple; Cháng Bǎi: whoever manages community property is the "head of the community," whoever manages temple property is the "grounds keeper"
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: the "head of the community" is a temple's abbot — one could call a board meeting and remove him. Master Cháng Bǎi: whoever manages community property is the head of the community; whoever manages the temple's property is the keeper of the grounds.

quiz.q: Regarding the exception for sexual conduct, what does the treatise say of renunciant bodhisattvas?
options: to protect the śrāvaka teaching from destruction, they should never engage in it at all
quiz.why: "Renunciant bodhisattvas, to protect the śrāvaka teaching from destruction, should never engage in non-celibate conduct at all." Master Cháng Bǎi: only lay bodhisattvas have this exception; renunciants do not.

quiz.q: "A woman presently belonging to no one" — how do the lectures explain "xiàn wú xìshǔ"?
options: not married to anyone and not under anyone else's protection
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: a woman who is not married to another and not under anyone else's protection is "presently unattached." Venerable Miào Jìng: she is not currently married.

quiz.q: Seeing beings bound to a harmful friend, what may the bodhisattva do without violation?
options: with a mind to benefit, speak divisive words to separate them from the bad friend
quiz.why: "Speaks words designed to divide the two, freeing the being from the harmful friend … with a mind to benefit, there is no violation and much merit." Master Cháng Bǎi: for instance, friends who use drugs or commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.
